*Translator's note:* *Heb* “after these things.” The words “the following episode took place” are added for stylistic reasons.

*Study note:* *King Ahab of Samaria*. Samaria, as the capital of the northern kingdom, here stands for the nation of Israel.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “if it is good in your eyes.”

*Text-critical note:* The Old Greek translation includes the following words: “And it will be mine as a garden of herbs.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Far be it from me, by the Lord, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers to you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “turned away his face.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “While I was talking…, I said…, he said….” Ahab’s explanation is one lengthy sentence in the Hebrew text, which is divided in the English translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “You, now, you are exercising kingship over Israel.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so your heart [i.e., disposition] might be well.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the nobles who were living in his city.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “did as Jezebel sent to them, just as was written in the scrolls which she sent to them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “led him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they stoned him with stones and he died.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Naboth was stoned and he died.” So also in v. {{1 Kings 21:15|15}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Jezebel”; the proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“she”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.
*Text-critical note:* The Old Greek translation includes the following words here: “he tore his garments and put on sackcloth. After these things.”
*Translator's note:* The words “of the property of the deceased” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Ahab said to Elijah.” The narrative is elliptical and streamlined. The words “when Elijah arrived” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (Elijah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you have sold yourself.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the eyes of.”

*Translator's note:* The introductory formula “the Lord says” is omitted in the Hebrew text, but supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Study note:* *Disaster*. There is a wordplay in the Hebrew text. The word translated “disaster” (רָעָה, raʿah) is similar to the word translated “evil” (v. {{1 Kings 21:20|20}}, הָרַע, haraʿ). Ahab’s sins would receive an appropriate punishment.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will burn after you.” Some take the verb בָּעַר (baʿar) to mean here “sweep away.” See the discussion of this verb in the notes at {{1 Kings 14:10|14:10}} and {{1 Kings 16:3|16:3}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and I will cut off from Ahab those who urinate against a wall, [including both those who are] restrained and let free [or “abandoned”] in Israel.” The precise meaning of the idiomatic phrase עָצוּר וְעָזוּב (ʿatsur veʿazuv, translated here “weak and incapacitated”) is uncertain. For various options see *HALOT* 871 s.v. עצר and M. Cogan and H. Tadmor, *II Kings* (AB), 107. The two terms are usually taken as polar opposites (“slaves and freemen” or “minors and adults”), but Cogan and Tadmor, on the basis of contextual considerations (note the usage with אֶפֶס (ʾefes), “nothing but”) in {{Deuteronomy 32:36|Deut 32:36}} and {{2 Kings 14:26|2 Kgs 14:26}}, argue convincingly that the terms are synonyms, meaning “restrained and abandoned,” and refer to incapable or incapacitated individuals.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “house.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “because of the provocation by which you angered [me], and you caused Israel to sin.”

*Text-critical note:* A few Hebrew mss and some ancient versions agree with {{2 Kings 9:10|2 Kgs 9:10}}, {{2 Kings 9:36|36}}, which reads, “the plot [of ground] at Jezreel.” The Hebrew words translated “outer wall” (חֵל, khel, defectively written here!) and “plot [of ground]” (חֵלֶק, kheleq) are spelled similarly.
*Translator's note:* “Dogs will eat the ones who belonging to Ahab who die in the city.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who sold himself.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the eyes of.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like Ahab…whom his wife Jezebel incited.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew word used here, גִלּוּלִים (gillulim) is always used as a disdainful reference to idols. It is generally thought to have originally referred to “dung pellets” (cf. KBL 183 s.v. גִלּוּלִים). It is only one of several terms used in this way, such as אֱלִילִים (ʾelilim, “worthless things”) and הֲבָלִים (havalim, “vanities” or “empty winds”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “He acted very abominably by walking after the disgusting idols, according to all which the Amorites had done.”

*Translator's note:* Or “humbles himself.” The expression occurs a second time later in this verse.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will not bring the disaster during his days, [but] in the days of his son I will bring the disaster on his house.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they lived three years without war between Aram and Israel.”
*Translator's note:* The word “visit” is supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Do you know that Ramoth Gilead belongs to us, and we hesitate to take it from the hand of the king of Aram?” The rhetorical question expects the answer, “Of course, you must know!”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Like me, like you; like my people, like your people; like my horses; like your horses.”

*Study note:* Jehoshaphat is requesting a prophetic oracle revealing the Lord’s will in the matter and their prospects for success. For examples of such oracles, see {{2 Samuel 5:19|2 Sam 5:19}}, {{2 Samuel 5:23|23-24}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Should I go against Ramoth Gilead for war or should I refrain?”

*Translator's note:* Though Jehoshaphat requested an oracle from “the Lord” (יְהוָה, Yahweh), they stop short of actually using this name and substitute the title אֲדֹנָי (ʾadonay, “lord; master”). This ambiguity may explain in part Jehoshaphat’s hesitancy and caution (vv. {{1 Kings 22:7|7-8}}). He seems to doubt that the four hundred are genuine prophets of the Lord.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to seek the Lord from him.”

*Translator's note:* Or “hate.”

*Translator's note:* The words “his name is” are supplied for stylistic reasons.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “were sitting, a man on his throne.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the words of the prophets are [with] one mouth good for the king.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “let your words be like the word of each of them and speak good.”

*Study note:* *“Attack! You will succeed; the Lord will hand it over to the king.”* One does not expect Micaiah, having just vowed to speak only what the Lord tells him, to agree with the other prophets and give the king an inaccurate prophecy. Micaiah’s actions became understandable later, when it is revealed that the Lord desires to deceive the king and lead him to his demise. The Lord even dispatches a lying spirit to deceive Ahab’s prophets. Micaiah can lie to the king because he realizes this lie is from the Lord. It is important to note that in v. {{1 Kings 22:14|14}} Micaiah only vows to speak the word of the Lord; he does not necessarily say he will tell the truth. In this case the Lord’s word itself is deceptive. Only when the king adjures him to tell the truth (v. {{1 Kings 22:16|16}}), does Micaiah do so.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (Micaiah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (Micaiah) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the spirit.” The significance of the article prefixed to רוּחַ (ruakh) is uncertain, but it could contain a clue as to this spirit’s identity, especially when interpreted in light of v. {{1 Kings 22:24|24}}. It is certainly possible, and probably even likely, that the article is used in a generic or dramatic sense and should be translated, “a spirit.” In the latter case it would show that this spirit was vivid and definite in the mind of Micaiah the storyteller. However, if one insists that the article indicates a well-known or universally known spirit, the following context provides a likely referent. Verse {{1 Kings 22:24|24}} tells how Zedekiah slapped Micaiah in the face and then asked sarcastically, “Which way did the spirit from the Lord (רוּחַ־יְהוָה, [ruakh Yahweh], *Heb* “the spirit of the Lord”) go when he went from me to speak to you?” When the phrase “the spirit of the Lord” refers to the divine spirit (rather than the divine breath or mind, {{Isaiah 40:7|Isa 40:7}}, {{Isaiah 40:13|13}}) elsewhere, the spirit energizes an individual or group for special tasks or moves one to prophesy. This raises the possibility that the deceiving spirit of vv. {{1 Kings 22:20|20-23}} is the same as the divine spirit mentioned by Zedekiah in v. {{1 Kings 22:24|24}}. This would explain why the article is used on רוּחַ; he can be called “the spirit” because he is the well-known spirit who energizes the prophets.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has two imperfects connected by וְגַם (vegam). These verbs could be translated as specific futures, “you will deceive and also you will prevail,” in which case the Lord is assuring the spirit of success on his mission. However, in a commissioning context (note the following imperatives) such as this, it is more likely that the imperfects are injunctive, in which case one could translate, “Deceive, and also overpower.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the bread of affliction and the water of affliction.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “come in peace.” So also in v. {{1 Kings 22:28|28}}.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verbal forms could be imperatives (“Disguise yourself and enter”), but this would make no sense in light of the immediately following context. The forms are better interpreted as infinitives absolute functioning as cohortatives. See *IBHS* 594 §35.5.2a. Some prefer to emend the forms to imperfects.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “now a man drew a bow in his innocence” (i.e., with no specific target in mind, or at least without realizing his target was the king of Israel).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (the king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “camp.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the king died and he came to Samaria, and they buried the king in Samaria.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “As for the rest of the acts of Ahab and all that he did, and the house of ivory which he built and all the cities which he built, are they not written on the scroll of the events of the days of the kings of Israel?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he walked in all the way of Asa his father and did not turn from it, doing what is right in the eyes of the Lord.”

*Study note:* Beginning with 22:43b, the verse numbers through 22:53 in the English Bible differ from the verse numbers in the Hebrew text (*BHS*) because 22:43b in the English Bible = 22:44 in the Hebrew text. The remaining verses in the chapter differ by one, with 22:44-53 ET = 22:45-54 HT.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “As for the rest of the events of Jehoshaphat, and his strength that he demonstrated and how he fought, are they not written on the scroll of the events of the days of the kings of Judah?”

*Study note:* Despite Asa’s opposition to these *male cultic prostitutes* (see {{1 Kings 15:12|1 Kgs 15:12}}) some of them had managed to remain in the land. Jehoshaphat finished what his father had started.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the rest of the male cultic prostitutes who were left in the days of Asa his father, he burned from the land.” Some understand the verb בִּעֵר (biʿer) to mean “sweep away” here rather than “burn.” See the note at {{1 Kings 14:10|1 Kgs 14:10}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Tarshish ships.” This probably refers to large ships either made in or capable of traveling to the distant western port of Tarshish.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Let my servants go with your servants in the fleet.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lay down with his fathers.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “with his fathers in the city of his father.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the eyes of.”

*Translator's note:* Or “way.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and walked in the way of his father and in the way of his mother and in the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat who made Israel sin.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he served Baal and bowed down to him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “according to all which his father had done.”
